initial.title: Spot trial expiry before it becomes a surprise
initial.body:
If you are running a small business, trial expiry is a simple workflow decision, not a grand AI project: when should a reminder fire, and who should see it first? The useful question is whether your trial dates already live in one place—calendar, email, spreadsheet, or CRM—or whether they are scattered across a few vendor accounts. If the dates are already central, a light monitoring rule may be enough. If they are scattered, you are probably looking at a small integration job, not a full overhaul.

The key control is human approval. Automation should surface the date; the owner still decides whether to renew, downgrade, or cancel. That matters because money movement and binding decisions should stay with a person. AI can help you notice the deadline, but it should not quietly choose the plan. That would be a very efficient way to buy the wrong thing.

A practical next step is to list every SaaS trial you are using and mark which tool, if any, already tracks the renewal date. That inventory tells you whether you need a simple reminder, a shared task, or a slightly smarter workflow in your own environment. Bareni’s approach starts with that one recurring workflow and keeps the decision bounded.

The abstract topic 'spotting trial expiry early' lacks substantive Bareni operational evidence. Replace general background with a concrete workflow decision: the owner's diagnostic question or threshold for deciding whether early-warning automation fits their business.

steps.instruction: Establish the concrete workflow problem: SaaS trials expire without owner notice, leading to service loss or surprise billing. Define the bounded scope as a single, repeatable monitoring decision—when to flag an expiry alert and to whom—not a multi-system integration.

State the diagnostic question the owner should answer: Is the trial-expiry data already in one digital tool (calendar, email, spreadsheet, or CRM), or scattered across multiple vendors? This determines whether simple monitoring suffices or API-based automation is necessary.

Explain the human-approval boundary: the owner must see the alert and decide whether to renew, downgrade, or cancel. Automation flags the date; the owner keeps authority. Reference Bareni's core principle that human approval precedes any money movement or binding decision.

Sketch two threshold scenarios: (a) trials 30 days out: email or Slack reminder to owner only; (b) trials 7 days out: escalate to a shared calendar or task list if the owner has not yet decided. Clarify that the owner sets the threshold based on business renewal lead time.

Note Bareni's hands-on delivery model: a pilot starts with a free diagnostic to confirm the workflow fits, then a fixed-price build in days to connect your tools and create the alert system. No strategy overhead or mandatory roadmap gates.

Close with a neutral next step: the owner should list the SaaS trials in use and note which tool (if any) already tracks renewal dates. This inventory informs the diagnostic and clarifies whether the work is simple monitoring or custom automation.

constraints_to_preserve.handling: No invented customer result, multi-person team, savings claim, or capability beyond the self-built demos and Bareni's stated consulting model. Treat the owner's SaaS renewal scenario as a shared workflow type, not a customer case study.

Emphasize that the owner retains authority over renewal decisions; automation surfaces alerts only. No autonomous payment or binding action. Respect Bareni's current scope: this is a straightforward monitoring workflow, not excluded high-sensitivity work.

Preserve the frozen persona (founder-to-founder, plain-speaking expert, trust over hype). Confirm that Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the thesis author, not yet a registered company, and deliver the bounded next step without implying production scale or customer deployments.

Use concrete diagnostic questions and threshold examples rather than general background. Keep the Bareni delivery model (free diagnostic, fixed-price pilot) distinct from speculative outcomes. No CTA; end with an actionable inventory step.
